params.text:
1. Define the result

The notebook asks you to write re_hits(pattern, candidates). It returns the complete input strings that contain a match, preserving their order and repeated entries. First establish what the result should contain before choosing operations.

Use pattern r"a" with ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "donut"]. Predict on paper, explain to a partner, then check. Switch roles on each page. Working alone? Write your explanation before checking.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both complete strings contain a. The function filters strings; it does not extract individual matches.
These are matching substrings. Return complete input strings instead.

answers.text: True, True, False, False in a list

params.text:
2. Follow a search result

Now investigate the decision that selects an input string. re.search(pattern, candidate) looks anywhere in the candidate. A successful search returns a Match object; an unsuccessful search returns None. An if tests the truth value of that result.

A Match object is truthy; None is falsy. Neither is itself the Boolean True or False. Converting a search result with bool() is valid but unnecessary in the condition.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: search looks anywhere. match checks the beginning; fullmatch requires the whole string.
match only checks the beginning. It would miss the a in pear.
fullmatch would require the entire string to match a.

3. Complete the flow

You have identified what a search returns. Now connect that result to a loop. Copy this flow onto paper and fill A, B and C before checking below.

  1. Start with an empty result list.
  2. Take the next candidate. If none remain, go to C.
  3. A: __________.
  4. If the search succeeds, B. Otherwise, leave the result unchanged.
  5. Return to step 2.
  6. C: finish the function.

The flowchart is written as numbered steps: the success and failure branches both return to the next-candidate step.

5. Explain and implement

You have specified the result, traced a search, and connected the branches. Now write your own re_hits() function in your course notebook. Do not copy a completed function from this activity.

  • Initialize a new list for each call.
  • Visit every candidate and decide whether to keep it.
  • Return complete original strings in input order.
  • Test an empty input, no matches, repeated entries, and a match inside a string.

Explain to your partner which operation decides whether to keep a string and which operation supplies the value being stored. Then switch roles and suggest a test that could expose a mistake.
